claim: Reaction times are assumed to reflect the underlying computations required for making decisions and preparing actions.
source: Reaction times (RTs) are assumed to reflect the underlying computations required for making decisions and preparing actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the common assumption in the field, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: Movements can be initiated earlier than typically expressed without affecting performance.
source: Recent work, however, has shown that movements can be initiated earlier than typically expressed without affecting performance
evidence: This claim references 'recent work' which implies citation to other studies.

claim: RTs are influenced by prior experience, specifically when a previously performed task required a specific RT to support task success.
source: we demonstrated that RTs are influenced by prior experience: when a previously performed task required a specific RT to support task success, this biased the RTs in future tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RT biases are similar to use-dependent biases observed for other movement parameters such as speed or direction.
source: This effect is similar to the use-dependent biases observed for other movement parameters such as speed or direction.
evidence: This draws a comparison to established phenomena in motor control.

claim: RT biases can occur without changing the underlying computations used to perform the action.
source: Moreover, kinematic analyses revealed that these RT biases could occur without changing the underlying computations used to perform the action.
evidence: This is supported by kinematic analysis data from the experiments.

claim: The RT is not solely determined by computational requirements but is an independent parameter that can be habitually set by prior experience.
source: Thus the RT is not solely determined by computational requirements but is an independent parameter that can be habitually set by prior experience.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The reaction time is the most widely used measure in neuroscience and psychology for noninvasively assessing processing in the brain.
source: The reaction time (RT) is arguably the most widely used measure in neuroscience and psychology for noninvasively assessing processing in the brain
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: RT is assumed to reflect the time needed to complete the perceptual and motor-planning computations required to prepare a response.
source: it is assumed to reflect the time needed to complete the perceptual and motor-planning computations required to prepare a response (Donders, 1969; Sternberg, 1969; Friston et al., 1996; Spivey, 2007; Sanders, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: RTs are modulated by stimulus complexity.
source: This assumption appears justified by evidence that RTs are modulated by factors such as stimulus complexity (Kaswan and Young, 1965; Hick, 1952; Ratcliff, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RTs are modulated by stimulus-response compatibility.
source: This assumption appears justified by evidence that RTs are modulated by factors such as stimulus complexity (Kaswan and Young, 1965; Hick, 1952; Ratcliff, 2002), stimulus-response compatibility (Fitts and Seeger, 1953; Simon and Rudell, 1967; Simon and Wolf, 1963)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RTs are modulated by the number of potential responses.
source: This assumption appears justified by evidence that RTs are modulated by factors such as stimulus complexity (Kaswan and Young, 1965; Hick, 1952; Ratcliff, 2002), stimulus-response compatibility (Fitts and Seeger, 1953; Simon and Rudell, 1967; Simon and Wolf, 1963), number of potential responses (Henry and Rogers, 1960; Fischman, 1984; Christina et al., 1982)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RTs are modulated by required response accuracy.
source: This assumption appears justified by evidence that RTs are modulated by factors such as stimulus complexity (Kaswan and Young, 1965; Hick, 1952; Ratcliff, 2002), stimulus-response compatibility (Fitts and Seeger, 1953; Simon and Rudell, 1967; Simon and Wolf, 1963), number of potential responses (Henry and Rogers, 1960; Fischman, 1984; Christina et al., 1982), or required response accuracy (Fitts, 1954; Fitts, 1966; Reddi and Carpenter, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Any reduction in RT should negatively affect the quality of the resulting response according to the assumption that RT reflects computation time.
source: According to this assumption, any reduction in the RT should negatively affect the quality of the resulting response.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the assumption that RT reflects computation time.

claim: Instructing participants to respond as rapidly as possible can lead to a decrease in accuracy.
source: Indeed, instructing participants to respond as rapidly as possible can lead to a decrease in accuracy (Fitts, 1966)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Changes in accuracy occur through direct manipulation of allowed preparation time.
source: consistent with changes in accuracy that occur through more direct manipulation of allowed preparation time (Schouten and Bekker, 1967; Ghez et al., 1997; Stanford et al., 2010; Haith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It was possible to reduce the RT considerably before any decline in movement accuracy was observed.
source: However, recent evidence showed that it was possible to reduce the RT considerably before any decline in movement accuracy was observed.
evidence: This references recent evidence from other studies.

claim: When individuals were placed under strict time constraints, movement accuracy and task success decreased only after the RT was shortened by ~80 ms.
source: For example, when individuals were placed under strict time constraints, movement accuracy and task success decreased only after the RT was shortened by ~80 ms (Haith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Startle by a loud acoustic stimulus could evoke initiation of a fully prepared action ~70 ms earlier than typically observed.
source: Similarly, startle by a loud acoustic stimulus could evoke initiation of a fully prepared action ~70 ms earlier than typically observed (Valls-SoleSolé et al., 1999; Carlsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The RT includes some additional time that is not required for computing the upcoming response.
source: These findings suggest that the RT includes some additional time that is not required for computing the upcoming response
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about RT reduction without accuracy decline.

claim: The RT is influenced by context.
source: An additional clue that the RT does not strictly represent computation time comes from evidence that the RT is influenced by context.
evidence: This introduces evidence from contextual studies.

claim: The RTs of simple point-to-point reaches were observed to be shorter than those of more complex curved movements.
source: In this study, the RTs of simple point-to-point reaches were observed to be shorter than those of more complex curved movements, consistent with the idea that RT reflects computation time.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Wong et al., 2016).

claim: When point-to-point movements were interleaved among curved reaches, the RTs of those point-to-point reaches were prolonged by ~90 ms, matching the RTs of the curved reaches.
source: However, when point-to-point movements were interleaved among curved reaches, the RTs of those point-to-point reaches were surprisingly prolonged by ~90 ms, matching the RTs of the curved reaches.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Wong et al., 2016).

claim: During a letter discrimination task, identifying letters that were presented upright occurred at much shorter RTs when all the letters were upright compared to when other letters in the same block of trials were rotated.
source: A similar contextual effect has been observed during mental rotation: during a letter discrimination task, identifying letters that were presented upright occurred at much shorter RTs when all the letters were upright compared to when other letters in the same block of trials were rotated (Ilan and Miller, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RTs might be subject to experience-dependent biases akin to other movement parameters such as speed or direction.
source: These data suggest that RTs might be subject to experience-dependent biases – akin to other movement parameters such as speed or direction (Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Verstynen and Sabes, 2011; Hammerbeck et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research on other movement parameters.

claim: RTs may be subject to habit in the sense that an RT of a given magnitude may become more likely to be generated in the future simply because it has been generated in the past.
source: That is, RTs may be subject to habit in the sense that an RT of a given magnitude may become more likely to be generated in the future simply because it has been generated in the past, regardless of current task requirements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the contextual effects described.

claim: Experience with initiating reaches at a short or long RT exerts a corresponding bias on the RTs of subsequently performed point-to-point reaches.
source: In the first experiment – a target-interception task – we showed that experience with initiating reaches at a short or long RT exerts a corresponding bias on the RTs of subsequently performed point-to-point reaches.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1.

claim: RT biases can occur for more complex curved reaches around barriers.
source: In a second experiment, we demonstrated that these RT biases can also occur for more complex curved reaches around barriers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The barrier task can be performed with or without the presence of a direct cue illustrating the appropriate trajectory, corresponding to greater or lesser computational requirements respectively.
source: This barrier task can be performed with or without the presence of a direct cue illustrating the appropriate trajectory, corresponding to greater or lesser computational requirements respectively (Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Participants' RTs in the cued condition depended strongly on whether or not they had previously experienced the uncued condition.
source: We found that participants' RTs in the cued condition depended strongly on whether or not they had previously experienced the uncued condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The observed experience-dependent changes in RT were not due to habitually ignoring the cue and planning the movements in a different manner.
source: Analysis of the kinematics of these curved reaches allowed us to determine that the observed experience-dependent changes in RT were not due to habitually ignoring the cue and planning the movements in a different manner
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Experience-dependent RT changes were due to habitually adopting a longer RT despite using a briefer computation to solve the task.
source: but instead to habitually adopting a longer RT despite using a briefer computation (i.e., taking advantage of the cue) to solve the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: The RT does not strictly reflect the time needed to complete the computations required for preparing responses, but may instead be selected habitually according to prior experience.
source: Together, these two experiments reveal that the RT does not strictly reflect the time needed to complete the computations required for preparing responses, but may instead be selected habitually according to prior experience.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from both experiments.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the outward-interception group had a pre-training RT of 295.38 ± 14.98 ms.
source: Pre-training	295.38 ± 14.98
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the outward-interception group had an RT of 255.20 ± 7.85 ms during the last training block.
source: Last training block	255.20 ± 7.85
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the outward-interception group had a post-training RT of 273.20 ± 12.10 ms.
source: Post-training	273.20 ± 12.10
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the inward-interception group had a pre-training RT of 290.76 ± 18.35 ms.
source: Pre-training	290.76 ± 18.35
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the inward-interception group had an RT of 564.82 ± 112.11 ms during the last training block.
source: Last training block	564.82 ± 112.11
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants in the inward-interception group had a post-training RT of 303.63 ± 17.25 ms.
source: Post-training	303.63 ± 17.25
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment reported in Table 1.

claim: At baseline, participants in both groups of Experiment 1 generated point-to-point reaches with comparable RTs.
source: At baseline, participants in both groups generated point-to-point reaches with comparable RTs (Table 1; no significant difference between groups: t = −0.22, p=0.82)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of baseline data from Experiment 1.

claim: When the target moved outward in Experiment 1, participants increased their movement speed relative to baseline.
source: When the target moved outward (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1 – Outward; Table 1), participants increased their movement speed (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = 6.30, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1 supported by data in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: When the target moved outward in Experiment 1, participants decreased their RT relative to baseline.
source: When the target moved outward (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1 – Outward; Table 1), participants increased their movement speed (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = 6.30, p<0.001) and decreased their RT (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = 2.99, p=0.02) relative to their behavior on baseline point-to-point reaches.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1 supported by data in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: RT reductions in the outward-interception task persisted in the post-training point-to-point reaching block.
source: These reductions in RT persisted in the final phase of the experiment when the target was again stationary: RTs during the post-training point-to-point reaching block were shorter than in the analogous pre-training block by 21.68 ± 6.32 ms (Figure 1C; paired t-test comparing post to pre, t(9) = −3.43, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1 supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The change in RT from pre-training to post-training in the outward-interception task was on average 76.6% of the total reduction in RT associated with the outward-interception task.
source: This change in RT from pre-training to post-training was on average 76.6% of the total reduction in RT associated with the outward-interception task (i.e., pre-training compared to the last outward-interception training block).
evidence: This is a calculated percentage based on experimental data.

claim: Changes in RT for point-to-point movements in the outward-interception task occurred with no significant change in peak velocity.
source: Importantly, these changes in RT for point-to-point movements occurred with no significant change in either peak velocity (paired t-test comparing post to pre, t(9) = 0.98, p=0.70)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Changes in RT for point-to-point movements in the outward-interception task occurred with no significant change in endpoint error.
source: Importantly, these changes in RT for point-to-point movements occurred with no significant change in either peak velocity (paired t-test comparing post to pre, t(9) = 0.98, p=0.70) or endpoint error (paired t-test comparing post to pre, t(9) = 0.95, p=0.70).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Repeatedly generating movements at low RTs led to a reduction of the RT on subsequent point-to-point reaches with no detectable decrement in performance.
source: Thus, repeatedly generating movements at low RTs led to a reduction of the RT on subsequent point-to-point reaches with no detectable decrement in performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the outward-interception data in Experiment 1.

claim: Training on the inward-interception task led to a decrease of movement speed relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline point-to-point movements, training on the inward-interception task led to a decrease of movement speed (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = −6.82, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Training on the inward-interception task led to an increase in RT relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline point-to-point movements, training on the inward-interception task led to a decrease of movement speed (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = −6.82, p<0.001) and an increase in RT (paired t-test comparing pre-training to the last training block, t(9) = 2.45, p=0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: RTs during a subsequent block of point-to-point reaches after inward-interception training increased on average by 12.87 ± 4.94 ms relative to baseline, although this change was not significant.
source: RTs during a subsequent block of point-to-point reaches increased on average by 12.87 ± 4.94 ms relative to baseline, although this change was not significant (paired t-test comparing post to pre, t(9) = 2.60, p=0.09)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The RT increase after inward-interception training corresponded to only 9.69% of the increase in RT observed during the interception task.
source: and corresponded to only 9.69% of the increase in RT observed during the interception task.
evidence: This is a calculated percentage based on experimental data.

claim: A mixed-effects model comparing the change in point-to-point RTs across the two groups in Experiment 1 revealed a significant interaction between the direction of target motion during training and the change in RT from pre-training to post-training blocks.
source: A mixed-effects model comparing the change in point-to-point RTs across the two groups revealed a significant interaction (likelihood ratio test; χ2(1)=77.55, p<0.001) between the direction of target motion during training (outward or inward) and the change in RT from pre-training to post-training blocks (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1 supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: The interaction in RT changes across groups in Experiment 1 was driven by a difference in RT only during the post-training block.
source: This interaction was driven by a difference in RT only during the post-training block (post-hoc test, p=0.03), since RTs during the pre-training block were comparable.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post-hoc analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: The RT can be biased in an experience-dependent manner.
source: Together, these data reveal that the RT can be biased in an experience-dependent manner, suggesting that the RT does not strictly reflect obligate computation time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 1.

claim: The presence of a path cue provides a significant RT advantage in the barrier task.
source: This task can be performed in one of two ways: either in the absence or presence of cues that illustrate a specific path around the barriers (Figure 2A). Although the movements required to complete the task are identical in both cases, the presence of a path cue has been observed to provide a significant RT advantage (Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and referenced in Figure 2A.

claim: The RT advantage from path cues is thought to reflect a difference in computational requirements between the cued and uncued conditions.
source: This advantage is thought to reflect a difference in computational requirements between the cued and uncued conditions, with the latter condition requiring an additional trajectory-planning stage to represent the path shape to be executed.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the RT advantage.

claim: Participants provided with a path cue exhibited a large RT advantage of 52.94 ms compared to individuals performing the task without the path cue in Experiment 2A.
source: Comparable to our previous findings (Wong et al., 2016), we observed that participants provided with a path cue exhibited a large RT advantage of 52.94 ms compared to individuals performing the task without the path cue (initial cueing condition experienced by each group; uncued: 349.76 ± 8.81 ms; cued: 296.82 ± 7.68 ms; main effect of condition, χ2(1)=500.61, p<0.001; Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: When the conditions were switched in Experiment 2A, the two groups exhibited similar RTs regardless of the presence or absence of the cue.
source: Specifically, whereas there was an RT advantage associated with the availability of a cue during the initial training block, when the conditions were switched the two groups exhibited similar RTs regardless of the presence or absence of the cue (cueing condition during the second block: uncued: 334.75 ± 8.17 ms, cued: 336.74 ± 8.01; χ2(1)=0.035, p=0.85; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a significant main effect of the order in which the cued and uncued conditions were experienced in Experiment 2A.
source: This experience-dependent effect of path cues on the RT was confirmed by a significant main effect of the order in which the cued and uncued conditions were experienced (χ2(1)=11.55, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: There was a significant interaction between condition and order in Experiment 2A.
source: as well as a significant interaction between condition and order (χ2(1)=105.42, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: The interaction in Experiment 2A arose because RTs were significantly longer on cued trials when participants had previously performed a block of uncued trials.
source: This effect could not be attributed to changes in the RTs of uncued trials performed first compared to second (p=0.25); instead, this interaction arose because RTs were significantly longer on cued trials when participants had previously performed a block of uncued trials (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post-hoc analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: Participants exhibited longer RTs on less computationally demanding cued trials if they experienced this condition second, even though they had more experience performing a more challenging version of the task.
source: Hence participants actually exhibited longer RTs on less computationally demanding cued trials if they experienced this condition second, even though they had more experience performing a more challenging version of the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical findings in Experiment 2A.

claim: The RTs in the cued blocks (but not the uncued blocks) exhibited a slow asymptotic decline across trials in Experiment 2A.
source: Interestingly, in Experiment 2A the RTs in the cued blocks (but not the uncued blocks) exhibited a slow asymptotic decline across trials (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The rate of RT decline in cued blocks was not different between the two groups in Experiment 2A.
source: The rate of decline was not different between the two groups (non-significant interaction between group and trial, t = −1.46, p=0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: Power-law fits to the time series of latencies in cued trials yielded similar exponents for both groups in Experiment 2A.
source: Power-law fits to the time series of latencies yielded similar exponents for both groups (cued trials experienced first: −0.025; cued trials experienced second: −0.029).
evidence: This is a result from fitting models to the data in Experiment 2A.

claim: A constant RT offset remained across the entire cued block in Experiment 2A, reflecting a strong, persistent RT bias for the group that had prior experience with the uncued condition.
source: Nevertheless, a constant RT offset remained across the entire block, reflecting a strong, persistent RT bias for the group that had prior experience with the uncued condition (t = 8.56, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: Task success in hitting the target while avoiding the barriers did not significantly vary with cueing condition or condition order in Experiment 2A.
source: In contrast to RT, task success in hitting the target while avoiding the barriers did not significantly vary with cueing condition or condition order (no effect of condition, χ2(1)=2.26, p=0.13; no effect of order, χ2(1)=2.50, p=0.11; non-significant interaction, χ2(1)=1.63, p=0.20).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: Participants who were exposed to the uncued condition first did not become more successful when they switched to the simpler, cued version of the task.
source: That is, participants who were exposed to the uncued condition first did not become more successful when they switched to the simpler, cued version of the task (uncued block: 81.97 ± 2.56% successful; cued block: 85.81 ± 1.62% successful; posthoc test, p=0.14)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: Participants who were first exposed to the cued condition did not become less successful when switched to the more difficult uncued task.
source: nor did participants who were first exposed to the cued condition become less successful when switched to the more difficult uncued task (cued block: 88.41 ± 1.66% successful; cued block: 88.02 ± 2.73% successful; posthoc test, p=1.00).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2A.

claim: While participants who initially performed the uncued condition exhibited prolonged RTs in the subsequent cued condition, this RT increase did not confer any performance advantage as measured by task success.
source: Thus while participants who initially performed the uncued condition exhibited prolonged RTs in the subsequent cued condition, this RT increase did not confer any performance advantage (as measured by task success) as might be expected by a speed-accuracy trade-off (Fitts, 1966).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the task success data in Experiment 2A, with reference to the speed-accuracy trade-off concept.

claim: In Experiment 2B, participants initially generated cued reaches at low RTs (pre-exposure cued block: 349.81 ± 36.03 ms).
source: Consistent with this prediction, participants in Experiment 2B initially generated cued reaches at low RTs (pre-exposure cued block: 349.81 ± 36.03 ms)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from Experiment 2B.

claim: In Experiment 2B, experience with performing a block of uncued trials led to prolonged RTs in the second cued block.
source: however, experience with performing a block of uncued trials (uncued-block RT: 390.26 ± 66.37 ms) led to prolonged RTs in the second cued block (post-exposure cued block: 375.09 ± 41.38 ms; effect of block, χ2(2)=532.46, p<0.001; significant differences between all pairs of blocks, p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2B supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in RT from the pre-exposure to the post-exposure cued blocks in Experiment 2B reflected an average RT bias of 80.98% of the change in the RT from the initial cued to the uncued block.
source: This increase in RT from the pre-exposure to the post-exposure cued blocks reflected an average RT bias of 80.98% of the change in the RT from the initial cued to the uncued block
evidence: This is a calculated percentage based on experimental data from Experiment 2B.

claim: RT is biased by prior exposure to the uncued condition even when participants had previously completed the cued task at low RT.
source: Thus, RT is surprisingly biased by prior exposure to the uncued condition in this task even when participants had previously completed the cued task at low RT.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 2B.

claim: The trajectories of movements planned using the cue should more closely resemble the path cues than movements planned de novo, regardless of the RTs at which these movements were initiated.
source: Specifically, we reasoned that the trajectories of movements planned using the cue should more closely resemble the path cues than movements planned de novo, regardless of the RTs at which these movements were initiated.
evidence: This is a logical prediction used to design the kinematic analysis.

claim: The presence of path cues significantly influenced movement kinematics in a consistent manner across participants in Experiment 2A.
source: We found that the presence of path cues significantly influenced movement kinematics in a consistent manner across participants: the shapes of the average trajectories for the cued and uncued conditions (pairs of blue and green lines in Figure 4A) were significantly different for at least one point along the length of the trajectory in 70% of all the target-barrier configurations performed (Figure 4A, significant differences between trajectory pairs along the movement are denoted by yellow dots).
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: For trajectories where differences were observed in Experiment 2A, on average 21% of the movement was found to be significantly different depending on the condition.
source: For those trajectories where differences were observed, on average 21% of the movement was found to be significantly different depending on the condition.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: There was no significant effect of the order in which the conditions were performed on movement kinematics in Experiment 2A.
source: However, there was no significant effect of the order in which the conditions were performed
evidence: This is a statistical finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: No kinematic differences were noted when comparing reaches performed in the same cueing condition in Experiment 2A.
source: moreover, no kinematic differences were noted when comparing reaches performed in the same cueing condition (i.e., between cued trials experienced first or second, or between uncued trials experienced first or second).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: Cued reaches were always executed in a similar fashion regardless of whether participants had prior experience with the uncued condition.
source: Thus cued reaches were always executed in a similar fashion regardless of whether participants had prior experience with the uncued condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: Reaches significantly resembled the path cue more closely when it was available in Experiment 2A.
source: In fact, a Procrustes shape-comparison analysis (Goodall, 1991; Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 1 – Procrustes Distance) revealed that reaches significantly resembled the path cue more closely when it was available (effect of condition: −0.13, 95% confidence interval: [−0.19,–0.08], Bayes factor = 0).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Procrustes analysis in Experiment 2A supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no significant effect of order on trajectory shape in Experiment 2A.
source: In contrast, there was no significant effect of order on trajectory shape (effect of order: −0.04 [-0.1, 0.02], Bayes factor = 14.24)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Procrustes analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: There was no significant effect of order on trajectory shape when comparing only cued trials in Experiment 2A.
source: even when comparing only cued trials (effect of order: 0.04 [-0.02, 0.09], Bayes factor = 13.63).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Procrustes analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: Participants used the path cue to simplify planning their movements whenever it was available.
source: Together, these data suggest that participants used the path cue to simplify planning their movements whenever it was available (Wong et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinematic analysis, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Participants were changing how they planned their movements in response to the cue, which resulted in quantitative changes in the kinematics of their actions such that movements more closely resembled the cued paths.
source: that is, participants were changing how they planned their movements in response to the cue, which resulted in quantitative changes in the kinematics of their actions such that movements more closely resembled the cued paths.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinematic analysis in Experiment 2A.

claim: In Experiment 2B, the kinematics in the second cued block resembled the path cues more closely than even those of the initial cued block.
source: Similar effects were observed in Experiment 2B (Supplementary file 1 for Experiment 2B kinematics analysis); in fact, the kinematics in the second cued block resembled the path cues more closely than even those of the initial cued block (effect of block: −0.04, 95% confidence intervals [−0.07,–0.02], Bayes factor = 0.39)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2B.

claim: Despite evidence suggesting that reaches were planned on a trial-by-trial basis in an experience-independent manner, RTs did not consistently reflect the computational benefit afforded by the path cue.
source: Hence despite evidence suggesting that reaches were planned on a trial-by-trial basis in an experience-independent manner (in particular by relying on the cue to plan the action), RTs did not consistently reflect the computational benefit afforded by the path cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing kinematic and RT data in Experiment 2.

claim: RTs exhibited an experience-dependent bias that was unrelated to how reaches were being planned and executed.
source: Instead, RTs exhibited an experience-dependent bias that was unrelated to how these reaches were being planned and executed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing kinematic and RT data in Experiment 2.

claim: The RT may be influenced by previous experience rather than strictly reflecting computation time.
source: Although the RT is typically assumed to directly reflect the computation time required to plan a movement (Donders, 1969; Sternberg, 1969; Friston et al., 1996; Spivey, 2007; Sanders, 1998), we demonstrated here that the RT may instead be influenced by previous experience.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, contrasting with cited prior assumptions.

claim: RT was influenced by recently generated RTs in the past even when those RTs were produced during another task with a different type of movement.
source: This was not simply a practice effect leading to more efficient planning of the same action; RT was influenced by recently generated RTs in the past even when those RTs were produced during another task with a different type of movement (e.g., in Experiment 1 the RTs of shooting movements to intercept a target biased the RTs of subsequent point-to-point reaches to stationary targets).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 1.

claim: The RT effect is comparable in magnitude to the RT changes previously observed in response to the addition of a delay period between stimulus and go cues.
source: This effect, while small, is comparable in magnitude to the RT changes previously observed in response to the addition of a delay period between stimulus and go cues (Churchland et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: The RT effect is comparable in magnitude to changes in stimulus or response complexity.
source: or to changes in stimulus or response complexity (Fitts, 1954; Fitts, 1966; Hick, 1952; Simon, 1967; Henry and Rogers, 1960, for review, see Teichner and Krebs, 1974).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: RTs can be modulated to be either shorter or longer than previously expressed depending on the nature of the interposed task.
source: Moreover, we showed that RTs can be modulated to be either shorter or longer than previously expressed depending on the nature of the interposed task
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of both experiments.

claim: RT biases persisted across a large number of subsequent trials.
source: and that these effects persisted across a large number of subsequent trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The RT expressed on any given trial may be lengthened or shortened (by 20–30 ms) strictly due to prior experience, with no other measurable impact on performance.
source: Thus in general, the RT expressed on any given trial may be lengthened or shortened (by 20–30 ms) strictly due to prior experience, with no other measurable impact on performance.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Experiment 1 provides clear evidence that the RT can be modulated in an experience-dependent manner as if by a habit.
source: Experiment 1 provides clear evidence that the RT can be modulated in an experience-dependent manner as if by a habit
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from Experiment 1.

claim: RT biases persist over a large number of trials.
source: and that such biases persist over a large number of trials.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1.

claim: Changing the duration of computational processes could increase task success, particularly when shortening the RT in the outward-interception task.
source: In the former case, changing the duration of computational processes could increase task success, particularly when shortening the RT in the outward-interception task.
evidence: This is a hypothetical scenario discussed in the context of interpreting Experiment 1.

claim: There was a motivational incentive that could drive changes in the speed-accuracy trade-off in favor of shortened RTs while maintaining consistent accuracy.
source: Thus there was a motivational incentive that could drive changes in the speed-accuracy trade-off in favor of shortened RTs while maintaining consistent accuracy (e.g., motivation could have driven an increase in the rate at which evidence accumulated in a drift-diffusion model of RT [Ratcliff, 1978])
evidence: This is a hypothetical explanation discussed with reference to a model.

claim: Reward can reduce RT without affecting accuracy.
source: much in the same way that reward can reduce RT without affecting accuracy (Takikawa et al., 2002; Hübner and Schlösser, 2010; Salinas et al., 2014; Manohar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The RT bias in Experiment 1 persisted across a large number of trials with no obvious decay toward the initially expressed RT.
source: First, the RT bias persisted across a large number of trials (e.g., the entire next block) with no obvious decay toward the initially expressed RT.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1 data.

claim: The persistence of RT bias stands in contrast to the short-lived effects of motivation, which appear to decay after only a few subsequent trials.
source: This persistence stands in contrast to the short-lived effects of motivation, which appear to decay after only a few subsequent trials (Takikawa et al., 2002; Xu-Wilson et al., 2009; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: The effect of motivation typically influences not just the RT, but also movement speed and accuracy.
source: Second, the effect of motivation typically influences not just the RT, but also movement speed and accuracy; in general, these three parameters have often been observed to modulate together in response to motivation (Takikawa et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No obvious changes in other movement kinematics such as movement speed or accuracy accompanied the RT biases in Experiment 1.
source: However, we observed no obvious changes in other movement kinematics such as movement speed or accuracy that accompanied the RT biases.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1 data.

claim: Motivation alone cannot account for the long-lasting RT biases observed in Experiment 1.
source: Nevertheless, these data suggest that motivation alone cannot account for the long-lasting RT biases observed in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of Experiment 1 in the context of motivational effects.

claim: Participants in the cued condition could have initiated their movements at short RTs during Experiment 2.
source: During Experiment 2, participants in the cued condition could have initiated their movements at short RTs
evidence: This is an observation about what was possible in Experiment 2.

claim: Participants exhibited persistently prolonged RTs in the cued condition when previously exposed to the more computationally demanding uncued condition.
source: however, they exhibited persistently prolonged RTs when previously exposed to the more computationally demanding uncued condition.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Movement kinematics changed in a consistent manner in the presence or absence of the path cues in Experiment 2.
source: In particular, we demonstrated that movement kinematics changed in a consistent manner in the presence or absence of the path cues, arguing that differences in movement kinematics do reflect changes in how these actions were being planned.
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: There was no effect of condition order on trajectory kinematics in Experiment 2.
source: However, we observed no effect of condition order on trajectory kinematics (i.e., reach kinematics were always influenced similarly by the path cues when they were available, regardless of whether participants had prior experience with uncued trials)
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Participants did not exhibit habitual cue-free preparation of the movement trajectory when generating reaches in the presence of a cue.
source: suggesting that participants did not ever exhibit habitual cue-free preparation of the movement trajectory when generating reaches in the presence of a cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from kinematic analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Movement kinematics indicate a particularly strong reliance on the cue to plan the action in the second cued block of Experiment 2B even though the RT did not reflect such changes in movement planning.
source: This is particularly evident in Experiment 2B, when movement kinematics indicate a particularly strong reliance on the cue to plan the action in the second cued block even though the RT did not reflect such changes in movement planning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing kinematic and RT data in Experiment 2B.

claim: Reaches in the uncued and cued conditions were confined to different portions of the workspace, making it unlikely that participants habitually applied the identical motor plans from previously-performed uncued reaches.
source: Moreover, reaches in the uncued and cued conditions were confined to different portions of the workspace, making it unlikely that participants habitually applied the identical motor plans from previously-performed uncued reaches.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design and its implications.

claim: Motor planning is determined by the current task at hand.
source: Hence these data suggest that unlike motor planning – which is determined by the current task at hand
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 2.

claim: Movement onset may be influenced in a use-dependent manner consistent with the idea of habitual initiation.
source: movement onset may be influenced in a use-dependent manner consistent with the idea of habitual initiation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 2.

claim: Movement onset may not represent the actual time required to prepare a movement.
source: and therefore may not represent the actual time required to prepare a movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 2.

claim: If the RT can be habitual, this implies that the time of movement initiation is not simply the end result of computational processing but may actually be represented as a separate movement parameter during the pre-movement period.
source: If the RT can be habitual, this implies that the time of movement initiation is not simply the end result of computational processing but may actually be represented as a separate movement parameter during the pre-movement period, analogous to movement speed.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Previous work has suggested that movement initiation may be independent of movement planning.
source: Indeed, previous work (Haith et al., 2016; Brown and Robbins, 1991) has suggested that movement initiation may be independent of movement planning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An initiation signature can be observed in motor cortex preceding movement onset in a manner that is independent of the specific action being prepared.
source: Such a distinction between planning and initiation is consistent with recent data suggesting that an initiation signature can be observed in motor cortex preceding movement onset in a manner that is independent of the specific action being prepared (Kaufman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The finding that movement initiation can be determined by prior experience, rather than the time when planning has completed, supports the view that initiation is independent of planning.
source: Our finding that movement initiation can be determined by prior experience, rather than the time when planning has completed, further supports this view.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in relation to prior work.

claim: Selection of RT based on prior experience rather than computation time implies that it should be possible to choose a RT that is too short to allow for all planning processes to be completed prior to movement initiation.
source: Selection of RT based on prior experience rather than computation time implies that it should be possible to choose a RT that is too short to allow for all planning processes to be completed prior to movement initiation.
evidence: This is a logical implication of the experimental findings.

claim: There are situations in which the RT is spontaneously chosen to be improperly short.
source: Consistent with this idea, there indeed appear to be situations in which the RT is spontaneously chosen to be improperly short (Orban de Xivry et al., 2017; Haith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Online corrections and refinements that occur after movement initiation help ensure a successful movement outcome when RT is too short.
source: In such cases, however, online corrections and refinements that occur after movement initiation help ensure a successful movement outcome (Orban de Xivry et al., 2017; Kohen et al., 2017; Wong and Haith, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the event that the RT is biased to be shorter than the time required to complete all necessary decision-making and planning-related computations, the motor system has online correction mechanisms in place to maintain overall task success.
source: Hence, in the event that the RT is biased to be shorter than the time required to complete all necessary decision-making and planning-related computations, the motor system has online correction mechanisms in place to maintain overall task success.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited research on online corrections.

claim: Experience-dependent biases have been previously demonstrated for movement parameters such as speed or direction.
source: Experience-dependent biases have been previously demonstrated for movement parameters such as speed or direction.
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in the field.

claim: Repetition of movements at a particular speed or toward a particular direction of the workspace strongly influences the kinematics of subsequently performed reaches.
source: For example, repetition of movements at a particular speed or toward a particular direction of the workspace strongly influences the kinematics of subsequently performed reaches (Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Verstynen and Sabes, 2011; Hammerbeck et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Repetition has been shown to influence the direction of movement invoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation.
source: Repetition has also been shown to influence the direction of movement invoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation (Classen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The influence of prior experience on movement biases appears for the most part to be short-lived, unlike the long-lasting effects seen in RT.
source: In these cases, however, the influence of prior experience on movement biases appears for the most part to be short-lived, unlike the long-lasting effects seen here in the RT.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior research.

claim: Experience-dependent biases may be a result of Hebbian learning.
source: It has previously been proposed that such biases may simply be a result of Hebbian learning (Bütefisch et al., 2000; Bütefisch et al., 2004): repetition of the same action presumably strengthens the neural circuits that give rise to that movement, making it more likely to be invoked in the future.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Experience-dependent biases have been framed in the context of a normative Bayesian model in which repetition leads to the construction of a strong prior that influences the preparation of future responses.
source: From a theoretical standpoint, experience-dependent biases have been framed in the context of a normative Bayesian model in which repetition leads to the construction of a strong prior that influences the preparation of future responses (Verstynen and Sabes, 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Explanations for experience-dependent biases rely on the assumption that the parameter in question is represented as a movement parameter that can be specified prior to movement.
source: Regardless of whether one uses a mechanistic or computational framework, however, explanations for experience-dependent biases rely on the assumption that the parameter in question – e.g., speed or direction – is represented as a movement parameter that can be specified prior to movement.
evidence: This is a general statement about theoretical frameworks for understanding biases.

claim: Experience-dependent biases on the RT imply that the RT is not simply the passive consequence of the time required to complete computational processing, but may instead be represented as a separate movement parameter that can be subject to habit.
source: Therefore, experience-dependent biases on the RT imply that the RT is not simply the passive consequence of the time required to complete computational processing, but may instead be represented as a separate movement parameter that can be subject to habit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the context of theoretical frameworks.

claim: Caution must be taken when interpreting differences in RT as indicative of the existence of computational stages with smaller or larger processing demands.
source: Thus, caution must be taken when interpreting differences in RT as indicative of the existence of computational stages with smaller or larger processing demands.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: RT differences may simply reflect carryover from RTs recently exhibited in the past (i.e., habit), regardless of computational demands.
source: Such RT differences may simply reflect carryover from RTs recently exhibited in the past (i.e., habit), regardless of computational demands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
